terms.definition: The keyword that declares a constant, a value that cannot be changed once it has been set.
terms.example: I made the greeting a let because it never needs to be reassigned.

terms.definition: The keyword that declares a variable, a value you can change after it has been set.
terms.example: The score is a var because it goes up every time the player taps.
terms.code:
var score = 0
score += 10  // Changing a var is allowed.
print(score)

terms.definition: The compiler's ability to work out a value's type from what you assign to it, so you do not have to write the type yourself.
terms.example: We left out the type annotation because type inference already knows it is an Int.
terms.code:
let count = 3       // Swift infers Int
let name = "Mina"   // Swift infers String
let price = 9.99    // Swift infers Double
print(type(of: price))

facebook.caption:
Quick Swift English for your day 👋

Today's 3 words:
• let: a constant. Set it once and it never changes.
• var: a variable. You can change it whenever you like.
• Type Inference: Swift works out the type for you, so you don't have to write it.

Every example is read twice, first at normal speed and then slowly, so you can say it out loud with me. Try the quiz at the end and share your answers in the comments!

Day 1 of iOS Daily English: 3 terms a day, from Swift basics to advanced iOS.

#iOSDev #Swift #LearnEnglish #SwiftUI

dialogue.title: First week: fixing the tip calculator

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Welcome to the team, Jake. Today we fix the tip calculator together.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Thanks, Mina. I see a lot of let and var in this file. How do I choose?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Use let when the value never changes. The tax rate is a good let.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And var is for a value that changes, like the total price?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. The total is a var, because it grows with every item.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Then I will write var taxRate, just in case.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Please do not. Someone can change the tax rate by mistake. Make it a let.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Oh, I see. A let protects the value, and Xcode stops me if I try to change it.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. And Xcode also warns you when a var never changes.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Good to know. Next question. Why did you write the tax rate with no type?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Because of type inference. Swift sees 0.08 and knows it is a Double.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So type inference does the work, and I do not write Double myself.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. But watch out. Did you write let count = 3 in the cart?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I did. Then I added 0.5 to it, and I got an error.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That is type inference again. It decided count is an Int, and 0.5 does not fit.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Got it. I will write 3.0, so Swift infers a Double.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Perfect. Now the discount is a var, and the rest is a let.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Nice. It looks cleaner already.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Great. Use let first, use var when you must, and trust type inference.
I made the tax rate a let, so nobody can change it.
